# SK3051 — The `async` method has no `CancellationToken` to forward

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `async` method that accepts no `CancellationToken` and calls something that would have taken one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Compilation |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

`SK3004` reports a token accepted and not passed on. This reports the step before it: the method accepts none, so there is nothing to pass on and no caller can stop the work. The two are the same argument at two points in the call graph, and applying this rule's fix is what makes `SK3004` reachable on the same body — a cancellation chain is worth nothing until it is complete, and the place it breaks first is the frame that never offered the parameter.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
async Task<string> LoadAsync(string path) {
    return await File.ReadAllTextAsync(path);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
async Task<string> LoadAsync(string path, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) {
    return await File.ReadAllTextAsync(path, cancellationToken);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The finding needs a call in the body that would have taken a token**, and that exemption is what separates a finding from advice. "Every async method should accept a token" fires on every leaf in every codebase; "this method calls something that offers a token and has none to give it" names a concrete cancellation that is broken, and the callee appears in the message. The call must match one of the two shapes `SK3004` can repair — an omitted *optional* `CancellationToken` parameter, or an overload that is this parameter list with a token appended and every argument positional — so the two rules cannot disagree about whether a call wants a token. ⚠ **`SK3004` and this rule are disjoint by construction, and the construction is the count**: `SK3004` fires only where *exactly one* token is in scope, this fires only where there are *none*. No body can satisfy both. ⚠ **A call inside a `catch` or a `finally` is not evidence**, because `SK3004` declines to forward a token into cleanup and reporting the method would leave a finding whose only repair the sibling rule then refuses. ⚠ **The rule is `Compilation`-scoped and the fix is what costs it.** Appending a parameter — even an optional one — breaks a method group conversion, because optional parameters do not participate in delegate conversion and `Func<Task> f = LoadAsync;` becomes CS0123. Whether a method is used that way is not visible in the file that declares it, so the analysis collects every name used as a method group across the compilation and reports only methods no such use names; the name check is over-broad on purpose, so any occurrence of the identifier in a non-invoked position silences the rule. The price is that the rule is not cacheable, which is the same trade `SK3001` states. ⚠ Not reported: `override`, `virtual`, `abstract`, `new`, `partial` and `extern` methods, interface implementations, anything carrying an attribute, `Main`, test methods, a parameter list ending in `params` (CS0231 leaves no edit), a method that already has a parameter named `cancellationToken`, and any method whose return type is not `Task`, `Task<T>`, `ValueTask` or `ValueTask<T>` — which is what keeps `async void` out of it. Generated code is excluded. The fix is unsafe because a parameter added to a signature is a signature the author should look at.
